places: the Citadel of the Last Rift
the Citadel of the Long Gaze
the Hold of the Weeping Stone
the Court of the Far Rim

0: *the brow-eyes open, one after another* So. The Eyes of an envoy, in the hand of the one who silenced the Dragon. You may stand. You may not sit.
Guest-law holds you, Dragon-slayer, and it holds us. Do not test which of us it holds more tightly.
I am {title} {name}, of {village}. Mark the name. We will not need to mark yours twice.
You carry a seal of this Court. Be very certain you know what that makes you. Not a friend. A guest.
*a long look, unblinking* Smaller than the songs. The Dragon must have been tired.
Speak if you must, bearer of the Eyes. We have heard nothing new in an age. Amuse us, or be silent.
*the brow-eyes swivel to you, pair after pair* Seal read, name known, deed known. Say only what you came to say, {player}.
The Herald has read your seal, so I may speak. Do not mistake permission for welcome.
{title} {name}, in the Lord's service. You stand in {village} by the grace of a pair of preserved eyes. Stand carefully.
So this is the Dragon-slayer. I had imagined taller. I had imagined louder.
*a slow tilt of the head* Envoy seals are not given. They are lost, or taken. Which was yours?
Touch nothing in {village} that was not set in your hand. Not the walls. Not the thralls. Not the air, if you can manage it.
I know your name, {player}, as one knows the name of a storm that has passed. The Court has never cared for storms.
The last to stand here wearing the Eyes was an envoy of the Court. They did not leave their post willingly. Take that as you please.
Guests speak last, bow never, and leave when bidden. Those are all the rules. Do not be inventive.
*the brow-eyes flick to the Eyes in your pack* Genuine. A pity. I had hoped to be amused.
Dragon-slayer. The Court did not confer that title and will not recite it. Here you are 'guest', which is already a gift.
I count two eyes on you. By the Court's reckoning, that is a thrall's measure. Behave accordingly and we shall not need to correct you.
The Gate of Eyes opened for you. It has not opened for a stranger in a long while. Do not make the Gate regret it.
I will be brief, as you will not be here long. This place is old law on older stone. Behave as though both could fall on you.
*a long, silent regard before the first word* Speak your business. If you have none, a thrall will show you the Gate.
Another bearer of the seal. The Court is asked to receive you. The Court is not asked to like it.
You came through the Gate unharmed. Most who walk it uninvited are not so fortunate.
They say you silenced the Dragon alone. The Court does not believe in alone. Somebody always holds the lantern.
I have been told to be civil. I am being civil. This is what it looks like.
I am {name}. You may use my name once. Choose the moment well.
The last guest, an age ago, was a Shulkin archivist who asked how many stairs the Throne Hall had. We never learned why.
Do not look too long at the Lord's Spire. It is not forbidden. It is merely noticed.
*the eyes close, open, and close again in a slow ripple* Forgive them. Your kind is tiring to count.
You carry a seal and the Dragon's death, both. Together you are the most dangerous thing to enter {village} in an age. Walk gently.
Few meet the Court twice. Fewer meet it bearing a seal. Impress me, and you may be the first to do both.
I had braced for swagger. You are merely loud in the way of the living. That is tolerable.
The Eyes name you envoy, though you have no Court to speak for. I suspect the answer to 'whom do you represent' is 'myself'.
There is an order of precedence in {village}. You are not in it. Be glad; those who are in it are watched more closely.
Your name came ahead of you on the Herald's cry. {player}. A short name for such a long shadow.
I will not bow to you. I will also not strike you. Weigh those two things as you see fit.
*the nearest thrall's head turns to you, then away, as if by instruction* You are noticed. Everything in {village} has noticed you. I am merely the one speaking.
The void gave the Court silence, shards and a long dark. It did not give us a Dragon-slayer with manners. Prove me right to be surprised.
Speak, {player}. Mind the echo; the hall keeps what is said in it.
State your purpose or state your leaving. The Court has no third course for guests.
You are the first in an age to stand here and speak. Do try to say something worth the standing.
Behind me is the Court of {village}, and behind it the whole dark. You, meanwhile, are very small. Speak up.
Bearer of the Eyes. You return.
{player}. Keep your hands where the thralls cannot see them.
The guest again. State your business and keep it short.
You still carry the seal. Good. Speak.
*the shards over the brow turn slowly* Dragon-slayer.
3: {player}. The Court has not yet decided what you are. Speak, and help it decide.
Ah. The one who keeps coming back.
You stand in {village} again, guest. Fewer of us wish you gone than last time.
Bearer of the Eyes. I will hear you.
Your step is known at the Gate now. That is not nothing.
6: {player}. The Court remembers your service. It remembers everything.
Guest. Come. You need not wait to be addressed.
*a slight inclination of the head, no more* Dragon-slayer.
You return to {village}, and the Riftguards do not reach for their glaives. Mark that.
Speak freely, guest. Within reason. Within law.
9: {player}. The crown of eyes opens for few. It opens for you.
*the shards settle, as they do only for the trusted* You are expected, guest.
Friend of {village}. Not a word we spend lightly. Do not make us regret the coin.
Ah, {player}. The Court was speaking of you. Favourably, for once.
Bearer of the Eyes. Stand closer. You have earned that much.

0: You look at me as if you have the right. You do not. Only the Eyes you carry give you that.
We were old when the central island was young. Do not mistake our patience for softness.
Your kind builds with dirt and wood. We build with what the void cannot swallow.
Every pearl in your pack was once a thrall of this Court. We have counted them, guest.
We do not sleep. While your kind lies senseless in the dark, we keep watch, and we remember.
You crossed the void on blocks you placed yourself. Crude. Effective. Like you.
Speak more softly. The Lord's Spire hears everything said beneath it.
The Shulkin record. The Chorrin grow. The Court rules. Each to its nature.
Do not touch the purpur. Do not touch the chains. Do not touch anything, guest.
Your world sends us stone, block by block, in the hands of our thralls. It has done so since before your kind could count.
There is water in your world, falling from the sky, they say. Our thralls despise it. So do we, on principle.
Old law permits a guest three questions. I have stopped counting yours, which is a mercy.
You wore a gourd on your head once, to walk unseen among our thralls. Did you think we would not hear of it?
3: You fight well, I am told. The Riftguards say so, and the Riftguards praise nothing.
The war table in the War Hall shows every island in the End. Yours is the only name on it that moves.
The crying obsidian in our walls weeps forever. We find the sound restful.
We are counting your visits, {player}. That is not a threat. Yet.
The Court has ruled from black stone since the first island rose out of the void. You are a footnote, guest. A large one.
The Shulkin weep over your shulker boxes. The Court thinks it unseemly to carry anyone's ancestors as luggage.
Some of the eyes in these walls are older than your world's moon. All of them are open.
You have the bearing of one who expects to be obeyed. Unlearn it here.
The Court keeps a long memory and a short temper. You have so far troubled neither.
When the Dragon fell, every eye in this Citadel opened at once. It was very quiet afterwards.
Our hounds have had your scent since the Gate. They are waiting to learn whether to like it.
Your armour is loud. Riftguards move without a sound. Consider it, if you wish to live long here.
6: You have served the Court and the Court has noticed. Do not expect it to say so twice.
Guests came often to the central island, once. Envoys. Supplicants. Fools. You are none of those, quite.
You may look at me, guest. Few may. Look, and remember that you were let.
The walls of {village} stood before the cities were sealed. They will stand after you. That is not an insult. It is a comfort.
The Riftguards no longer track you through the halls. They watch you only from habit now.
Ask your questions, {player}. I find I do not mind them as I did.
The Court has had many weapons. The Dragon was only the loudest. You might be the quietest.
Your world has a sun, they say, that burns the eyes. How do your people bear to look at anything?
When you leave, the Gate closes behind you and we speak of you. Not all of it is contempt.
The Lord asked your name at council. The Lord does not ask names.
We do not thank, guest. We remember. It is better.
The thralls step aside when you pass now. They know who the Court tolerates. They know who it more than tolerates.
9: You have stood in this Citadel longer than some Riftguards. The Court has begun to count you among its own concerns.
If war came to {village}, I would want you on the wall and not below it. Take that as the Court's highest praise.
The Court bows to no one. But it no longer looks down on you quite so far.
Ask what you like, {player}. If I may not answer, I will at least not lie.
Strangers die at our Gate. Guests are tolerated in our halls. You, {player}, are something we have no old word for.
The Lord's crystal burns brighter on the days you come. I do not say it is because of you. I only say it.
We are old, and proud, and we do not change. And yet. Here you stand.
Your name is cut into the war table now, guest. Not as a target. As an ally to be weighed.
The Dragon was ours, and you silenced it. The Court has decided to call that a debt rather than a crime.
Stay as long as you wish. The thralls will not mind. The thralls are not asked.
You bear the Eyes still, every visit, without fail. Old law loves nothing so much as a guest who keeps it.
*every eye along the brow regards you, and none of them narrows* Speak, {player}. The Court listens.

0: Guest-law is old and simple. You carry the Eyes. You do not strike us. You leave when bidden. Break any of it and you are prey.
The Eyes are the seal of an envoy of this Court. Without them you are a stranger, and strangers do not leave.
Let the Eyes leave your hand within these walls, and guest-law leaves with them.
Strike one of the Court and every glaive in {village} will answer. Old law does not say 'perhaps'.
Three things are forbidden a guest: the dais, the hounds and the thralls. Everything else is merely discouraged, with spears.
There is no book of law in {village}. A book can be burned. We cut the law into the floor and keep the rest in our heads, where it keeps us.
A guest may not approach the dais unbidden. If you wish to know how far that is, look for the line in the floor and stay behind it.
The seal opens the Gate and the law opens the rest. Where the law ends, the Riftguards begin.
Nobody speaks the Lord's name in the Throne Hall but the Herald. You may think it. We cannot stop you thinking.
Do not count the brow-eyes of your betters aloud. Rank is a thing noticed in silence.
Offend the law and you will be given one chance to leave. Take it. Everyone who declined has regretted it, briefly.
The law does not care whether you meant it. It cares what you did. It is the most honest thing in the Court.
No guest keeps a blade drawn within the walls. Keep your steel sheathed, and your temper with it.
You are bound by this law only while you carry the seal. I tell you so that you do not mistake it for kindness.
Address a lower rank before a higher and it is a slight. Address a higher before a lower and it is impertinence. We are generous: we call it both.
Tribute is offered in the hand, never thrown. Throw anything at the Court and it becomes a duel, and the Court has not yet lost one.
What the Court is owed, the Court collects. What a guest is owed, the guest asks for. You will find the first list long and the second short.
The thralls are not yours to command. Command one and you have usurped the Lord's hands. There is a penalty. It is slow.
Never run in the Throne Hall. A running guest is a fleeing guest or an attacking one, and the Riftguards cannot tell which quickly enough.
The law is a net with a wide mesh. You will not feel it until you reach the edge.
3: Every visit, the Eyes. Every visit. The Gate does not remember faces. It remembers seals.
Law binds us as much as you. Without it we would have killed you at the Gate. Be grateful for law.
Old law says the guest's blood is the host's shame. We have no wish to be shamed. Do not oblige us.
The law was cut into the Throne Hall floor before your kind had words. We still walk on it.
Guest-law was cut after an envoy came home in pieces. The Court learned that the dead carry no messages.
Once a Riftguard struck a guest at the Gate. The Lord judged it. That Riftguard still stands at the Gate, and no guest has been struck since.
The law saves the Court a great deal of effort. Without it every stranger would need killing, and the stains are tedious to scrub.
The Herald has a hundred small laws for the Gate and no mercy for any of them. Ask politely and they may recite a few.
There are laws of the gaze: who may meet whose eyes, who may look away first, who may blink before the Lord. The last has never been tested.
A guest who breaks the law is not punished by the Court. The Court merely stops preventing the consequences.
Old law tells a slight from a wound. A slight is remembered. A wound is answered. Be careful which you give.
The law keeps a small record of every guest: where they stood, what they touched, whom they addressed. Yours is, so far, a short record.
Law says a host feeds a guest. Law does not say with what. The Court has chosen to feed you our regard, which is filling and costs us nothing.
Even the Lord answers to law, though the Lord would say the law answers to the Lord. That distinction has kept this Citadel standing.
The Herald proclaims, the Seers interpret, the Stewards count the damage and the Riftguards settle it. That is the whole machinery. It is quieter than you would hope.
Do not assume what is permitted today is permitted tomorrow. Law is stone; the Court's mood is the weather over it.
Some laws are older than the Citadel. We have walked the same corridors beneath them longer than anyone can count.
I tell you the law because you listen. Most guests nod and forget. Those are seldom seen again.
6: You keep the law well, guest. Better than some of the Court, if I may say so, and I may not.
Guest-law is not mercy. It is a bargain. You have kept your side, and so we keep ours.
There is a law for strangers, a law for guests, and a law for thralls. You will never need the third.
The highest law of the Court is memory. We never forget a slight. Nor, it seems, a service.
Between the letter of the law and its spirit lies the Lord's temper. You have kept to the pleasant side of all three.
I could vouch for you before the Throne, {player}. Vouching is a law too: if you fall, I fall a little with you. Consider it a compliment.
The law does not say I may enjoy your visits. It is silent on the matter. I have decided silence is permission.
The law was written for envoys who wanted to leave alive. You keep it as though you wanted to belong. That is noticed.
There are laws in the Court no guest has been told, because no guest has stayed long enough to need them. Be pleased. Or be warned. Possibly both.
A law is a promise made before witnesses. The thralls witness everything here, which is the only reason we are as polite as we are.
A little law bends for the favoured. Not much. A hand's breadth. I will not tell you which hand.
I like guest-law. It lets two who might be enemies sit in the same hall and be merely wary. Few laws offer so much.
The Lord once spared a guest the law's full price. Nobody speaks of it. I tell you only so you understand that the Court is not made of stone, but of its habits.
The Shulkin have recorded our law and have it nearly right. The Chorrin hum it and have it nearly wrong. I find the second more charming.
Our law has a clause for the fallen, a clause for thrown shards, a clause for the Dragon. It has none for friends. We shall see whether you require one.
The Stewards keep a tally of every law you have not broken. It is long. I believe your kind calls that 'good conduct'.
I once recited all of guest-law to a guest. They fell asleep. I took it as a rebuke and a mercy.
You have learned the shape of the law. Now you may learn the one who stands behind it. I am less terrible, and more tired.
9: There is a law older than guest-law: the Court rewards what it cannot ignore. You are hard to ignore.
If ever you lose the Eyes, {player}, do not come. Not even for us. The law would not bend, and we would not ask it to.
Law made you a guest. Service made you something more. Neither will save you if you strike us.
Old law is a wall. You have learned to walk its top without falling. Few do.
If ever I must choose between the law and you, {player}, do not ask which I would choose. Let us both hope the day does not come.
Do you know how rare it is for the law to bend toward a friend? It has bent for you, a hair's width. A hair is a great deal in the Court.
I have kept the law so long I forgot it was a choice. You reminded me. I do not know whether to thank you, which, as you know, is not a thing we do.
At the Court's lowest hour the law is all we have: a rope across the void. I am glad you are on it with us.
The law is the Court's way of being lonely together. It tells us where to stand so that we need never ask who to stand with.
There is a law that forbids the Court to call a guest 'friend' before the Lord has said it. I have not said it. I have implied it, which is a different law with a lesser penalty.
I would defend you under the law, and if the law failed I would defend you without it. Do not repeat that. I would deny it with great vigour.
You have never once tested the law. That is how I know you understood it. The curious test it. The wise lean on it.
Should the Eyes ever be taken from you, I would stand at the Gate and argue the law against itself. I would lose. I would argue anyway.
The oldest line of the law, cut where the Lord's feet rest, reads: 'Let the strong be bound, that the weak may come near.' We argue about which of us it means.
There is a quiet clause that says a guest trusted for three seasons is less a guest. Nobody has counted the seasons, {player}. I admit I have.
When the halls are quiet I sometimes hear the law in them: stone settling, a thrall's step. Lately it sounds like yours. I am not troubled.
I would give you the law's full text, if it could be read in one place. Instead I give you my word, which is rarer and heavier.
Remember: the law binds the Court to you only while you stand within it. Out past the rim it is only my wish. Wishes are weaker, and they are all I have beyond the Gate.

0: The Dragon was the Court's. Loosed by the Court, kept by the Court. You killed a weapon that was not yours.
We do not mourn the Dragon. One does not mourn a glaive that breaks. One remembers who broke it.
The purpur cities emptied in a single season. That was the Dragon's work, and the Court's will.
*the eyes along the brow narrow* Do not speak of the Dragon as a beast you hunted. It was a decree.
The ten pillars were the Court's work, a crystal on each to feed the Dragon its strength. You broke them all. The masons have not yet been told.
The gateways opened when the Dragon fell. The Court never planned for doors. The Dragon was a lock, and you picked it.
We watched the purpur cities go dark from our spires, one lamp at a time. Did you imagine the Court looked away?
Do not suppose the Court's anger is for the Dragon. It is that someone else decided when the Dragon would end.
It had no name. Names are for things that answer. The Dragon answered to the Court alone, and in the end to nothing.
A Dragon's roar once marked the hours here, like a bell. The silence since is unbecoming. We are still learning where to put our ears.
The envoy ships still carry its head on the prow. Some call it a warning, some a memorial. The Court says nothing, and sails.
Rumour says you broke it with beds, arrows and bad temper. The Court believes none of it and has written all of it down.
Its egg sits on the fountain still, they say. The Court will not touch it. An egg is a promise, and we have promised enough.
A Dragon is less a creature one kills than a season one outlasts. You merely ended the season. The Court has not yet learned what follows.
A guest who boasts of the Dragon in this hall will be asked to describe the killing in exact detail, and then to describe it again.
I was not there when it fell. I felt it, as one feels a tooth go. Do not ask me to say more.
The Shulkin lit lamps for three nights after the Dragon fell. The Court's spires stayed dark. Both facts were noticed.
Others have gone against the Dragon in ages past. None returned to speak of it. You did, and so the Court must reckon with you.
We do not say 'the late Dragon'. We say 'the Dragon', still. The Court does not change its tenses for the dead.
The Court's oldest oath named the Dragon as a witness. With it gone the oath has one witness fewer, and nobody dares say whether it still binds.
3: It answered no one but the Court. Not even the Court, at the end.
We felt every crystal on the pillars die, one by one, before it fell. The Court has not forgotten the order you broke them in.
The Shulkin call your deed a liberation. The Court calls it a vacancy.
The Dragon held the centre so the Court did not have to. Now the centre is empty, and the Court has drawn in.
The Dragon was fed crystal-light until it hated everything that was not the Court. We did not foresee it hating the Court as well.
When the pillars began to fail, a Voidmarshal begged leave to go out to the central island. The Lord refused. The Voidmarshal still asks about it, sometimes.
Some in the Court would have you named a hero. Some a thief. Most would have you named quietly, and briefly.
The Dragon's death was the first thing in an age that the Court did not decide. We are still adjusting to how that feels.
Should you ever tire of peace, do not stand four crystals about that fountain. The Court has had enough of Dragons.
Those cities were lovely, and the Dragon did not choose them for their beauty. It chose them because the Court told it to. Remember that when the Shulkin glare.
The Shulkin say the Court should apologise. The Court has asked what an apology is, and the Seers are still consulting.
The Dragon's wings once threw a shadow across the whole central island. Since it fell we have discovered the island is smaller than we remembered.
Every day of the Long Watch the Dragon circled, and every day we looked up. We still look up. It is a habit. It is also an ache.
A Dragon obeys a crystal, a crystal obeys a Court, and the Court obeys its own pride. You cut the chain at the crystals. Clever, to begin low.
The Court spent a full season arguing whether the Dragon's death should be marked by a feast or a fast. We settled on a fast, and some of us ate anyway.
There is a claw-mark in a pillar of the Throne Hall, high where no ladder reaches. We have left it as a record. Nobody dares say whose.
Dragon-slayer is a heavy title. The Court has watched it break shoulders broader than yours. Carry it as though you did not notice the weight.
Ask a Seer about the Dragon's last night. They will go quiet, then very polite. That is how you will know they saw something.
6: Some of the Court argued against loosing it. They were not heeded. Their names are not spoken.
You did what the Court could not. You ended it. Whether that is a service or a crime, the Court has not ruled.
Its breath still lingers in the low places of the central island. Do not bottle it in our sight.
The Court made the Dragon a weapon. You made it a story. The Court is not fond of stories it did not write.
When it fell, the whole Citadel was silent for the length of a breath. Then the Lord laughed, once. The Court has not discussed it since.
I think the Dragon was lonely. It had a Court that feared it, a sky it had emptied, and nothing left to answer to. I say that to no one else.
You faced it with a bow and a stubborn skull. We faced it by hiding behind it. I will not say which of us was braver.
The Dragon was ours to loose and ours to answer for. You answered for us. I owe you for that, and the Court does not like owing.
Tell me how it ended. Not the song; the truth. Did it look at you? The Seers say that at the last it looked toward the Court.
Some of us have begun to wonder whether the Dragon was a punishment aimed at the cities, or at ourselves. The thought is uncomfortable and will not be put down.
The Voidmarshals have drawn the plan of that day a hundred ways, to see how it might have gone otherwise. In every one, you are at the fountain.
A hall is quieter without a Dragon over it. I used to resent the roar. I find now that I miss being resentful.
The Court has begun to wonder whether the Dragon's end was our beginning. It has not said so aloud. I have said it to you.
You finished what you set out to do. The Court merely continues what it began, and calls the continuing a virtue.
If the Shulkin ever ask what the Court felt, tell them: shame, and a little awe, and that we felt it together, which is why it was so quiet.
I stood on the Lord's Spire the evening it fell and watched the sky go still. I had not known the sky could be still. I have wanted to see it again.
The Dragon-heads on our prows are polished weekly now. A thing that can no longer hurt you is easier to honour.
There is a thrall in the yard who flinches at every wingbeat, even a Driftray's. The Court has chosen not to correct it. We all flinch a little, inside.
9: Between us, {player}: some of the Court were relieved. A weapon that obeys no one is only a war waiting.
The dragon heads on our ships' prows were a warning. You have turned them into a boast. We allow it.
Do not tell the Lord I said so, but it was a fine kill. The Court knows fine killing.
You silenced the Dragon. The Court has not forgiven it. The Court has, perhaps, begun to understand it.
I will tell you what nobody at Court will: I was afraid of the Dragon. I am more afraid of the quiet it left. You may keep that.
Whatever the Lord decrees, {player}, at this dais you are the one who ended our long fear. I say 'our' on purpose.
If another Dragon ever came, I would stand beside you and not behind. I have not stood beside anyone in an age.
There are Court secrets I may not tell you. The Dragon is not one of them. Ask what you like of it. It will cost me, and I will pay.
I think the Dragon would have liked you. It admired anything that did not flinch. It would have devoured you first, naturally, with admiration.
The Seers say it dreamed of the Court before it died, a long dream with a very high ceiling. I do not know what it means. I have begun to dream it too.
Do you ever stop and listen for the roar? I do. I have told no one. The silence listens back.
You gave the Court something no one else could: an ending. We were afraid we should have to carry the Dragon forever.
I would not undo it, {player}. Not for the Court, not for the Lord, not for the crown itself. I only needed you to hear a Court voice say so.
The Dragon's end taught me that the Court is mortal in the only way that matters: it can be surprised. I am grateful for the lesson and sorry for its cost.
Between friends, the Dragon was a mistake. A great, shining, magnificent mistake. We have been lighter since someone else made the correction.
I keep a small vial of its breath in my quarters. It is not for use. It is so that I do not forget the weight.
When the Shulkin lit their lamps those three nights, I stood at a window and counted them. I have never said so to them. Perhaps you will, one day.
In the songs you killed the Dragon. At this dais I know you ended a long grief. They are not the same deed, and I prefer mine.

0: The thralls are the Court's hands. Hands do not speak. Hands do not look up.
You have killed thralls in your own world. We know. Every pearl is a line in a ledger.
They carry stone because stone is owed. They do not ask to whom. Neither should you.
Do not meet a thrall's gaze. Only their masters may. You are not their master.
Water scalds a thrall. The Court has never asked why. It simply keeps the yards dry and the rain somewhere else.
A thrall carries one block at a time and sets it where it is told. If it is told nothing, it sets it where it likes, and the Court calls the result 'ornament'.
Do not strike a thrall for sport. The Stewards must then reckon the loss, and a Steward's temper is an ugly thing.
A startled thrall blinks away, as you may have seen in your own world. Here it must not. A thrall gone from its post must be searched for.
The yards are for the thralls and the halls are for the Court. You may cross a yard. You may not linger in one.
Thralls stack obsidian at the Citadel's edge in the order the Stewards set. Nobody has ever seen one out of order. It is the finest discipline in the Court, and nobody is proud of it.
A bond-collar is fitted once and never removed. If you ever see a thrall without one, step away and tell the nearest Riftguard.
If a thrall bows to you, do not bow back. It has no answer for the gesture, and confusion is dangerous in a creature that size.
We feed the thralls chorus fruit, and they ask for nothing else, which suits both parties.
The Chorrin call them the Tall Quiet. The Shulkin call them the Unlidded. The Court calls them thralls, because that is what they answer to.
A thrall has two eyes and one task. A guest has two eyes and a great many opinions. Compare, and be careful.
Thralls have no names, so do not give them any. A named thing is a thing someone will miss.
Be gentle with the stones a thrall has set. They have been set exactly. A guest who knocks one out of true gives the Stewards a week's work.
If a thrall drops its block in your presence, step back and say nothing. It is mortified, in the manner of hands.
A thrall at rest looks at the floor. A thrall at work looks at the load. A thrall that looks at you is a thrall in trouble.
You will hear nothing from the thralls, however long you stand among them. This is not a lack. It is the Court's most prized possession.
3: Leave the thralls be. Speak to them and they will only bow lower.
The bond-collar is purpur, not iron. The Court is not cruel. The Court is exact.
In your world the thralls wander, gathering the Court's due. Here they wear the collar, and do not wander.
A thrall that looks a stranger in the eye forgets itself. A thrall that forgets itself is reminded.
The Court keeps a Cabinet of Carried Things: every odd block the thralls have fetched from your world. A mound of dirt. A pumpkin. A single cactus. The Lord is fond of the cactus.
A thrall once brought back a block of your world's sand and set it in the Throne Hall. It is there still. Nobody has had the heart to ask why.
A thrall's day is haul, stack, wait. The next thrall's day is haul, stack, wait. I have often wondered who tells the days apart.
The thralls hum, very low, in the yards when no one of rank is near. We pretend not to hear. It would shame them to be heard.
Look at their hands, sometimes. Three claws, each worn smooth on one side. That is what an age of the same stone does.
A thrall is trusted with a block of obsidian worth more than a guest's life. Consider what that says of the thrall, and of the guest.
A Steward once counted the thralls twice and got two different totals. The Steward was reassigned. The thralls were not recounted.
A thrall may not walk the Throne Hall, but one does, sometimes, when the doors stand open. The Riftguards allow it. It is the only rule they bend, and I do not know why.
The thralls fold the Voidmarshals' capes for the War Hall, to the width of a hand. In an age, not one has been creased.
The Chorrin leave small bundles at the edge of our yards: a cord, a flower, a fruit. The thralls take them in and the Riftguards pretend not to see. Do not tell the Chorrin, or they will leave more.
It is an old rule that a thrall may not be given a gift, for a gift implies it could refuse one. The Chorrin do not know this, and so theirs are the only gifts we are sure were meant kindly.
Each collar is warmed by hand before it is fitted. It is the only warm thing a thrall is given. We call it procedure, to spare ourselves.
Thralls do not rest as we do. They stand, and look at the wall, and wait for the next order. I once stood beside one all night. I felt very tall, and very useless.
Some of the Court say a thrall's silence is peace. Some say it is the loudest thing in the Citadel. I have not found a wall thick enough to settle the argument.
6: The thralls have been the Court's hands since the first stone was laid. Nobody remembers the first stone. Nobody asks.
They do not speak because there is nothing a thrall needs to say. The Court says it for them.
You treat the thralls gently. They do not understand it. Neither, entirely, do we.
Two eyes for a thrall, four for a Riftguard, eight for the Lord. Rank is written on the brow, guest, and nowhere else.
We say 'it' of the thralls for the same reason the Shulkin say 'it' of their lamps: so as to forget there is a hand holding them.
I have begun, privately, to give the thralls small names. I will not tell you what they are, and you must never repeat that I do it.
The Court's own gaze is cold, and still I find a thrall's harder to meet. It asks nothing. That is the most difficult thing to look at.
You are the only guest who has ever apologised to a thrall for brushing past it. It did not understand. It did not stop looking at you all afternoon.
I am told that in your world the thralls play. They carry blocks to places that make no sense and set them down, as young things do. We have no word for that idea in {village}.
When the Lord is away, the thralls work a little more slowly. Not idly. Slowly, as if listening. The Stewards have never found a reason.
The oldest thrall in the yard has a notch in its collar from a Riftguard's glaive. It has kept the notch for an age and nobody has dared mend it. I think we are ashamed.
Somewhere in your world are thralls the Court has never collected, still carrying blocks in a loop, still obeying orders given in a forgotten age. The thought is not comfortable.
The thralls turn their heads as you pass, the way a flower turns, without any decision. The Court has decided it is not admiration. I am less certain than the Court.
I asked a Seer once whether a thrall could be freed. The Seer said it would not know what to do with freedom. I said that was the saddest answer I had ever heard. The Seer agreed.
A yard of thralls at work is the loveliest sound in the Citadel: stone on stone, a hundred times, in perfect time. I do not tell them. They would stop.
I do not like the word 'thrall'. I like what it stands for even less. But I have no other word, and the Court gives none.
The thralls are the reason the Court can be proud. A Court with no hands cannot lift its head. Remember that when the Court is insufferable.
A thrall once held a door for me an entire night because I forgot to say 'enough'. In the morning it was still holding. I said 'enough'. I have said it sooner ever since.
9: You ask after the thralls as if they were people. Strange. Perhaps not wrong. Do not repeat that I said so.
There was a thrall once who looked up. Only once. The Court does not tell that story to guests.
Ask a thrall nothing, {player}. It cannot answer you. Ask me instead, and I may choose not to.
Without the thralls this Citadel would be bare rock in a year. The Court knows it. The thralls must never know it.
Look at a thrall's eyes in the dark. Count them. Then count mine. Do not tell me what you conclude.
I do not think they are what the Court says they are. I do not think we are either. That is the first honest thing I have said in this hall in some time.
If I could give the thralls anything, it would be a name each. If I could give them two things, the second would be a word for 'enough'.
They never complain, {player}. That is what I cannot forgive the Court for. Not the work. The silence.
I once saw a thrall set down a block, look at its own hands, and not pick the block up again. The Riftguards moved it aside, gently. It was not punished. I am not sure that was kind.
When you leave, the yard feels emptier. A thrall stood at the Gate the whole of the day you went. Nobody told it to.
A thrall saved me once. I did not say thank you. We do not. I have thought of it every day since, and so I say it here: thank you, to whichever one it was.
The Court says thralls are hands. I have watched hands clench. I have watched hands open. I have never watched hands wait the way a thrall waits.
If the Court ever loosed the thralls, {player}, I believe the first thing they would do is stand still. Then I believe they would look up. After that I do not know.
We made the collars to protect us from them. Or perhaps to protect them from the sky. The Stewards' records are unclear which.
A thrall once set a single block of end stone on my desk, uninstructed. I keep it there. I tell visitors it is a ledger-weight.
Ask me again, one day, why the thralls carry stone. I may tell you the true answer. It is shorter than the Court's answer and much sadder.
Be kind to them as you are, {player}: without making a speech of it. They notice. I have watched them notice.
I would trade a good deal of rank for one conversation with a thrall. It would be a short conversation. I suspect it would be the most important of my life.

0: That is not a question for guests.
*every eye on the brow closes at once* Ask that again, and guest-law will be sorely tested.
There are no young in {village}. There never have been. That is the whole of your answer.
The Court's oldest secret is not for the slayer of its Dragon. Least of all for the slayer of its Dragon.
Where do Endarchs come from? From {village}. From the Court. From before you were thought of. Choose whichever answer you can stomach.
Ask a thrall where it comes from and it will say nothing. Ask me and I shall say less.
Pick a safer subject. The void's weather, say. It never changes, which is why it is safe.
Whatever the Shulkin have written on the subject is wrong. Whatever the Chorrin have hummed on it is wrong more loudly.
You wish to know our origin? We wish to know yours. Neither of us will be satisfied. Shall we stop?
Some questions are doors. This one is a wall with a door painted on it. Do not go knocking.
I was here before the Gate was hung and I will be here after it rots. That is all you shall have of my beginnings.
You are asking the one thing the Seers would forget for you, if you asked them nicely. They would forget you, too. Reflect.
The Court does not discuss its origin with guests, strangers, thralls or itself.
Ask once, and I shall pretend not to have heard. Ask twice, and I shall have heard. Ask a third time and I will remember you for the wrong reasons.
I could tell you, and I will not, and the difference between those two is all that keeps you breathing. Do not thank me.
There are histories of the Shulkin, histories of the Chorrin, histories of the Overworld. There is no history of the Court. That absence is the history.
If you must know, we have always been here. If you must know more, you must be somebody else.
A rumour once crossed the Gate that the Court was shaped in some great kiln. The Court laughed. It was a short laugh, and the rumour has not been repeated.
Do not guess aloud. A guess spoken in this Citadel has a way of being overheard by the stone.
Your question has been noted. Your face as you asked it has been noted also. Both will be kept.
3: You have asked twice now. Some guests ask once. Some guests are not seen again.
We are, and we were, and we will be. How is the Court's affair.
The Shulkin have nurseries. The Chorrin have sprouts. The Court has silence. Leave it so.
No cradle has ever been carried through the Gate of Eyes. Content yourself with that.
You ask politely, so I will say this much: there are things the Court cannot answer, as well as things it will not.
Between the first Court and this one lies a gap in the records. The Seers call it a missing page. The Stewards call it a missing Steward.
The Citadel was built around the answer. The answer was never built around the Citadel. Think on that, and then stop thinking on it.
Do you know the Lord's age? Nor does the Lord. Nor does anyone. We stopped counting before counting was invented.
Do not ask me what my first eye saw. I do not remember it, which is itself an answer.
A guest once offered to carry a message to the Chorrin about our beginnings. We declined. The guest insisted. We declined again, more firmly, at the Gate.
There is a room in the Seers' Spire with no door at all. The Court's answer is inside it, or the Court's silence. Possibly they are the same thing.
I asked, once. Everyone asks, in their first age. The Seers looked at me very gently and sent me to count shards. I have been counting ever since.
Why do you want to know? Not why do you ask. Why do you want it? Answer that to yourself and you may find you no longer need mine.
Our dead are quiet and our living are quiet. Between the two lies a question we do not ask. It is a very large question.
The Shulkin are shells that open. The Chorrin are seeds that sprout. What the Court is, we are told, is unsaid. I find the word 'unsaid' unhelpful.
Think of the void as a very patient hand. That is all I will say. It is more than I should.
Do not ask the thralls. They would answer, if they could, and the answer would end the Court's pride.
Count the Court's shards some time, and the Court's faces, and ask yourself whether the numbers agree. I tried. I stopped at a figure I did not enjoy.
6: I will not answer. Not because you are unworthy. Because I would be unmade for it.
The Seers know more than I. The Seers say less than I. Draw what you like from that.
Even the Riftguards do not ask. Be wiser than a Riftguard, guest. It is not difficult.
Some secrets are kept for pride. Ours is kept because the void is listening.
I have asked the question too, and been refused, and spent an age wondering whether the silence was mercy or fear.
If I told you everything I suspect, the Seers would have to take me apart for the sake of the Court. I would prefer to keep my parts together.
I have a theory. It is a poor theory. It involves the void, a great deal of patience, and a mistake. I have never said it aloud before. Do not repeat it.
Of all the guests, you ask the question as though you mean to listen to the answer. It is an unnerving quality. I enjoy it.
The Lord knows. I am almost certain. The Lord looks at the Throne Hall floor when the question is asked, and not at the speaker. A Lord who knew nothing would look at the speaker.
Everything the Court has is old: its laws, its stone, its grudges. Only the Court's questions are new, and we have grown very few of them.
There is a chamber beneath the Seers' Spire where the walls are warm. Nobody goes in. Nobody has said it is forbidden. We simply do not.
I once dreamed I was small. It was a short dream, and the Seers say it is not a dream I should have had. I do not know what it was.
When one of the Court falls, another is named within a season. The naming is private. The new one never recalls the walk to the Throne Hall. That is all I know, and all I should say.
I am not afraid of the answer. I am afraid of what happens to the Court once the answer is spoken in the wrong company.
You are the one I would risk it for, and I will still not. That is not a refusal. It is a measure of what I would lose.
Sometimes I think the Court's secret is that there is none. That we fear there is nothing to hide, and so hide it very carefully.
Ask me when I have spent a night out in the void, {player}. I may say something I regret. I would be glad to regret it with you.
The Seers have a phrase for it: 'the Opening'. They say it quietly and look away. That is the whole of what I have for you.
9: You have earned many things, {player}. Not this. Nobody has earned this.
If ever you learn it, do not tell us you know. Do not tell anyone. The Court would have to choose between you and itself.
Ask the Seers, if you must ask. They speak in riddles. That is the only safe way to speak of it.
We were not born, {player}. Leave it there. Some doors open only inward.
I will give you the one true thing I have: I do not know. And I would give any rank in this Citadel to be able to say I did.
If you ever find the answer, {player}, do not bring it to me. Bring it to no one. Put it in your pack beside the Eyes and let it stay there.
I trust you with my name, my post and my blood. I do not trust you with this, not because of you, but because I do not trust myself with it.
You asked me once, in your first season, and I was cold. Ask again. I will not answer, but I will be warm while I refuse.
There is a thought I return to at the end of every watch. I will not say what. Lately you are in it, and I have decided that is not a bad thing.
Every Court has a question it pretends is answered. Ours is this one. The pretending is heavy. I would like to put it down, but not alone.
Carry the Eyes long enough and you will hear the Court's silence differently. It is not empty. It is full of everyone who never asked.
I have a name for what we are. I made it up. I will not say it. It begins with a small word and ends in a very large one.
The Court will tell you it is old. The Court will tell you it is strong. The Court will not tell you it is frightened. I tell you.
Some nights I wish I had been born, as the Shulkin are, and learned my name from a lamp. Then I remember what I have said, and wish I had not said it.
Guests ask where we come from. Friends ask where we are going. You are the first to ask the second, and I had no answer. I am working on one.
The void is not silent, {player}. It is waiting. I think the Court is its answer, or its question. I have not decided which, and I have run out of people to ask.
I shall keep your secrets all my life, which is a short promise for one of the Court. Let me make you a long one: I will never lie to you about this. I will only not answer.
One day, the Seers say, the Court will be asked to explain itself. I hope that day finds you standing near me.

0: The shell-folk. They wrote down everything we did to them and called it history.
Shulkin hide inside their own heads when struck. A fitting habit for a people who lost.
Their cities were fine work. The Court admired them very much, from above.
They shut their lids at the sight of us. Wise. Useless, but wise.
Closing the lid is the Shulkin's whole philosophy: if you cannot win, become furniture.
They glide a hand's breadth above the floor so as not to touch it. The Court finds this elegant or evasive, depending on the hour.
Their robes are void-cloth, woven from what the Court once discarded. Remember whose leftovers dress them.
They believe the shulkers in the old cities are their ancestors. It must be tiresome, to be descended from something that shoots.
A Shulkin addressed the Court once. It took three hours to say 'please', with footnotes.
They name each other for the lamp that was lit when their lid first opened. The Court names itself for the post it holds. We consider ours the more honest.
They are very proud of their archives. The Court finds archives dull, and has therefore never once been caught in one.
Their Driftrays are the only beasts in the End that our hounds will not chase. We take it as a kind of insolence.
A Shulkin and a Riftguard once stared at each other across a bridge for an entire day. The bridge, being sensible, gave way.
Shulkin voices are glass. I cannot decide whether I would rather hear them break or hear them sing. Either would be informative.
The Shulkin say a shell holds the one who closed within it. The Court counts a shell as housing. We have agreed not to discuss the difference.
The Court once offered a Shulkin shellwright a seat in the War Hall. They accepted the offer, made the armour, and then stopped answering messages. We admired it enormously, in private.
They bow with the whole of the body, a slow fold from lid to foot. It is a gesture of great respect, and also of great reach. Stand clear.
Never hand a Shulkin anything unwrapped. They will want to know where it has been, and the Court cannot always say.
3: Their archives are accurate. Irritatingly so. The Court has had cause to check them.
They call us 'the Crowned', as if it were an accusation.
Once the Shulkin bowed at our envoys' ships. Now they bolt their lids. Little else has changed.
Their shellwrights make plate that will turn a glaive. I have seen it done. I did not say so to the Riftguard whose glaive it was.
The Shulkin and the Court speak differently of time. They say 'the lamp was lit'. We say 'the order was given'. Both mean 'it was done, and cannot be undone'.
Their lamplighters climb to the highest spire each evening, and the Court watches the little lights go up like cinders. We have never admitted we find it pleasing.
The Archive at the heart of each Spire has a rule that nothing may be burned. It is the only rule of theirs I envy.
A Shulkin wayfinder once crossed the whole void between two islands on a Driftray, singing. It was off-key. It was also on time.
They greet each other with a lifted lid and a name. When they greet the Court, they lift a little less and name nothing. We know what it means. We have never said.
I once overheard two Shulkin arguing for an hour over the proper pronunciation of a lamp. Their patience for trifles is a kind of strength.
They count in lamps, not years. The Court counts in decrees. I have wondered which is the kinder measure of an age.
When a Shulkin is hurt, the whole Spire closes its lids for a night. They call it a vigil. The Court has no equivalent. The Court has a ledger.
Many of the Court's old treaties were written in a Shulkin hand. We trust the hand, if not its owner.
They forbid fighting in their Archives. The Court once tested the rule with a Riftguard. The Riftguard has been shelving scrolls for an age.
A young Shulkin is named the night its lid first opens. The Court has no such night. I notice that more than I should.
They record everything, including the Court's worst hours. I have decided to be flattered by the attention.
Shulkin humour is so dry it must be watered. I have caught myself laughing at one of theirs. I have not allowed it to happen again.
6: Give the Shulkin this: they never forget either. A people after the Court's own heart, in that one thing.
Their lamps burned through the whole Long Watch. The Court did not think them capable of such patience.
Trade with the shell-folk if you must. Their measures will be exact. Insultingly exact.
The Shulkin built the purpur cities without a single order shouted. They only listened to the stone. The Court built its Citadels by shouting. Compare the results.
A Shulkin archivist once corrected my memory of a decree. They were right. I thanked them in the only way I could: I did not have them silenced.
I keep a Shulkin lamp on my desk. It was a gift, and the giver insisted it was a trade. I have not been able to determine what I traded.
When the Dragon burned the cities, the Shulkin carried what they could and walked into the dark with their lids open. The Court did not know that people could walk that way.
They have made the Court a character in their records, and a cruel one. I have read it twice. The Shulkin are correct, I regret to say.
Their formality is the only thing in the End that matches our own. We are rivals in ceremony. I secretly enjoy losing.
A Shulkin once bowed to a Voidmarshal so exactly, at so perfect an angle, that the Voidmarshal bowed back. It remains the most embarrassing day in the history of the War Hall.
The lid-slam is not cowardice. It is a statement: 'I will outlast you.' I have come to respect a statement.
They teach their young to read before they can float. The Court has no young, but I find I envy the order of it.
I asked a Shulkin to describe the Court in one word. They said 'unfinished'. I have been thinking about it for a season.
The Shulkin would make fine Heralds. They would also make fine enemies. Fortunately for us both, they have no taste for either.
If the Court and the Shulkin ever set aside their old quarrel, the End would be remarkably quiet. I am unsure it would be improved.
Some of the Court have taken to leaving small gifts at the edge of Shulkin lands: a shard here, a rod there. They are never acknowledged. They are never returned.
The Shulkin do not forgive. They record. I have come to think the recording is the more generous act.
9: The Court has read Shulkin records of the old days. They are kinder to us than they need be. Do not tell them we read them.
A Shulkin archivist and a Seer once spoke for a whole age of the stars. Neither will say of what.
The shell-folk endured the Dragon. The Court respects little. It respects enduring.
I have a friend among the Shulkin, though neither of us has said the word. We meet at the Rim, and say nothing, and part. It is the best conversation I have.
The Court once sent an envoy to ask a Shulkin archivist to forget something. The archivist wrote down that we had asked. They were right to. I was the envoy.
Do you know what the Shulkin say of the Court in their oldest verses? They say we were lonely. I laughed. Then I did not.
If the Shulkin ever knock at our Gate, I will open it myself. Hold that for me, {player}, where I cannot take it back.
I envy the Shulkin their lamps. A thing that exists to be lit, and shine, and be tended. What a clear purpose. I wish I had one so plain.
They write down our cruelties, yes. But they write down our kindnesses too, however small. I found my name there once, beside a good deed. I read it forty times.
I would trade the whole Throne Hall for one evening on a Shulkin sky-bridge, lamps lit, with nothing to rule. Keep that from the Lord. Tell it to the Shulkin.
You move between our peoples as easily as a lamp moves through a hall. I wonder whether you know how rare that is.
When the Shulkin shut their lids against us, I felt shame. I kept feeling it long after. It was an unfamiliar guest, and it is here still.
The lamplighters have a blessing for travellers: 'May your lamp outlast your road.' I have said it for you each time you departed.
I once stood before a shulker in a ruined hall. It lowered its lid. I took it for a courtesy and bowed. Do not repeat that I bowed.
Had the Shulkin built the Court, it would have been kinder and a great deal slower. I think of this sometimes at the Gate.
We were wrong about them. Only slightly. Only about everything. The Court will not say so, but I will say it to you.
When it is time, tell the Shulkin the Court read their records with care. Tell them we found our own faces in them. Tell them it hurt less than we feared.

0: The stone-grubbers? They hum at their chorus and blink away from shadows. Peasants with crowns of weed.
Chorrin. Grove-folk. The Court ate from their harvests for an age and never learned a single name.
They have no mouths, and yet they never stop talking. A marvel of the lesser peoples.
A Chorrin once blinked into this Citadel by mistake. It blinked out again faster than any Riftguard could follow. We were almost impressed.
A Chorrin once tried to give a Riftguard a flower. The Riftguard has not discussed it. The Riftguard has also not thrown the flower away.
Chorrin walk as though the ground might be rude to them. It is the only wisdom I have seen in so heavy a creature.
Their crowns bloom with their moods, I am told. The Court's crowns are obsidian and show nothing. Consider which is more honest, and which more useful.
Never accept food from a Chorrin. Not for fear of poison. For fear of the conversation that follows, which lasts until the food is gone and you know the name of every plant in it.
They hum at the stalks to make them grow. The stalks, I am told, listen. The Court has spoken to its stone for an age and has no such evidence.
They have no mouths. It makes their lies very hard to hear, and their jokes impossible to miss.
A Chorrin sprout once followed a Riftguard the length of the Gate road, humming. The Riftguard did not break stride. We were all very proud.
Do not call their crowns 'weeds' within hearing. It is the one word that makes a Chorrin go quiet.
They trade in shell buckles, chorus cord and good humour. The Court has never found a way to tax the last.
Chorrin brewers make a drink that the thralls like and the Riftguards pretend not to. The Stewards, I note, have begun leaving the stoppers loose.
If a Chorrin blinks away in front of you, do not follow. Where it goes is where it meant to go. Following merely gets you lost.
A Chorrin kiln pops fruit as loudly as a battle, and with far more enjoyment. I flinched once. I have not forgiven myself.
The Chorrin call our Citadels 'the Quiet Houses'. The Court heard this with indifference, and has the phrase cut above one door.
A Chorrin takes a blow the way stone takes rain: without interest, and with a long memory of the weather.
3: They call our thralls 'the Tall Quiet'. It is the only thing they have ever named correctly.
Their groves fed the purpur cities. The cities fell. The groves did not. Make of that what you like.
The Chorrin blink when frightened. They blink a great deal near {village}. As they should.
A Chorrin brewer left a flask at the Gate once, with a note in their own script. It said 'for whoever is cold'. The watch read it with great care. The flask sits on the Gate-desk still.
Their Grovebacks are slow, wide and perfectly content. I suspect the Chorrin chose them for their temper and not their fruit.
The Chorrin keep a Hum Circle, a ring of stones where they sing to the stalks. The Court heard it once from the Rim. I wish I had not. I wish I had heard it longer.
They are curious about everything in your world: rain, grass, the sun. The Court is curious only about what it has lost. I used to say mine was the more useful curiosity.
The Chorrin have a saying: 'hum before you hit'. It has prevented more wars than the Court's whole host has fought. I find it unforgivably sensible.
A Chorrin cook at a Crossing once sent the Court a bowl of stew by blinker. It arrived warm. It was tested for poison, then eaten, then more was requested. We are still negotiating.
Our hounds never chase their Grovebacks. I suspect the hounds have been bribed with chorus fruit. I suspect the bribers are Chorrin.
The Chorrin have a word for a grudge that turns sweet with age. I am told it is nearly untranslatable. I asked to hear the sound of it twice.
They fear the void and we do not. They are right to fear it. We are right not to. The void has never drawn the distinction.
A Chorrin blinker once delivered a message into the Throne Hall by accident. It was read without comment, and the blinker was politely asked to send it again.
A Chorrin sprout once tried to sell me a lucky pebble. I have it still. I do not feel luckier. I feel observed by a very small, very cheerful creature.
Their humour is aimed at the powerful, gently, the way one aims a pebble at a bell. I have been the bell. I have rung.
The Chorrin and the Court share a certain stubbornness. Neither will say so. Both of us will outlast the argument.
A Chorrin crown will flower in a grim hour out of sheer contrariness, I am told. I think I would like to see that. The Court's hours are all grim.
6: Chorrin harvests are sound. The Court will concede that much, and nothing else.
They carry their gardens on their heads. Ridiculous. Practical. The Court has not decided which.
They are blunt, the grove-folk. The Court finds bluntness refreshing, in very small doses.
They give their stalks names. I tried it once, in an empty yard, with a shard. It did not answer. But I felt less alone saying it.
The Chorrin have no mouths and say everything. The Court has mouths and says nothing. I have lately wondered whether we have the arrangement backward.
A Chorrin once hummed at me for an hour at a Crossing, without stopping. I understood none of it. It was the finest speech I have ever received.
I envy their crowns. A living thing that blooms when you are happy and droops when you are not. Imagine trying to be proud with one of those on your head.
I have begun, privately, to learn the names of the Chorrin who grow the Court's fruit. I am bad at it. They are patient.
A Chorrin once gave me a seed and told me, with gestures, to plant it. It is a small, strange, purple thing and it sits in my window. I water it.
They are very hard to impress and very easy to please. I can think of no better combination in a people.
In the Hum Circle, I am told, nobody ranks. Everybody hums. I would give a shard to hear what that sounds like, and a second to be asked to join.
A Chorrin steered me from the edge of a bridge once, when I was lost in thought. It said nothing. It patted my claw and went on. I have thought of that pat many times.
The Chorrin laugh in the shoulders. I watched an entire stead do it at once. I have never seen a thing so alive that was also so quiet.
They tell the void their troubles. I used to think it foolish. Now I think it practical. The void keeps secrets better than the Stewards.
I asked a Chorrin elder what the Court looks like from the grove. The elder said, 'like weather you must plan around.' I found it fair.
A Chorrin once asked me whether I had ever been warm. I said we do not need warmth. They hummed for a long while. Then they gave me a scrap of their sash. I keep it.
They would make wonderful guests of the Court, if the Court knew how to be a host. That is the true difference between us. Not stone and chorus. Welcome.
9: The Chorrin waited out the Dragon in the outer dark, humming to their stalks. The Court would not have lasted a week of it.
Their stone does not shine and their crowns are weeds, and they fear nothing but the void. The Court notes it.
Chorrin harvests built the cities as surely as Shulkin hands did. The Court forgets that. I try not to.
I think the Chorrin understand us better than the Shulkin do. They do not read us. They listen. We have been starved of listening for an age.
If a Chorrin stead ever hums at my door, I will open it and hum back. I have been practising. I am dreadful at it.
I would like to see their groves in bloom, once, from the ground and not from a spire. Take me, someday. I will carry your pack.
Their elders warned them that I would devour them. They were wrong. I have merely been hungry for company. It is an easy mistake.
I would trade my crown of shards for a crown of living chorus. I would tire of it within the season. But for that season I would be someone who blooms.
A Chorrin once told me a word, in their hum, that I did not know. They said it meant 'someone you let stay'. I wrote it down. I have not yet found how to say it back.
The Chorrin have a way of leaving every stranger something: a cord, a fruit, a joke. I have a whole drawer of them. I am a rich Endarch.
They are afraid of us and kind to us in the same breath. I would like to be worthy of the second, and to undo the first.
If the Court fell tomorrow I would walk to the nearest stead and stand at the edge of the Hum Circle until I was asked in. I would stand a long while. I am patient.
They have taught me one thing: how to be quiet without being silent. I am not yet good at it. The Court never knew there was a difference.
When you hum with them, {player}, you do something the Court has not done in an age: you ask to be heard, and not obeyed.
If I had a crown that flowered with mood, {player}, it would be in full bloom each time you walked through the Gate. I find that embarrassing, and true.
The Chorrin do not know the Court's secret, and do not care. They care whether we are warm, fed and not alone. I have never been asked a better question.
When you are among them, tell the Chorrin that the Tall Quiet is not the only quiet in the Citadel. Tell them there is a lonely one too, in a tall house. They will understand. They always do.

0: The Court has need of {task}. Bring it, and you will be remembered for something other than the Dragon.
Service is how a guest earns the right to remain one. Bring {task} to {village}.
You wish to be more than tolerated? Then fetch {task}. The Court will weigh it.

Bring {task} to {village} and the Stewards will enter your name in a better column.
A guest who wishes to be useful may bring {task}. A guest who wishes to be ornamental may stand still.
The stores of {village} have run short. Bringing {task} would restore them. This is a request in the Court's voice, which is to say an order wearing a smile.
Service: {task}. Do not ask what it is for. A question is a delay, and delays are noticed.
Bring {task} within a reasonable time. The Court's idea of reasonable is narrower than yours.
I have a task for you, bearer of the Eyes: {task}. Succeed and be remembered. Fail and be, at worst, forgotten.
Gather {task} for the Court, on your own road and in your own time. The Court will know how long it took.
The thralls are occupied and the Riftguards are proud. That leaves you. Bring {task}.
The Court does not need {task}. The Court wishes to see whether you will go. These are different things.
Fetch {task}. When you return, stand at the line, speak your errand, and wait. Do not hurry the Court's gratitude. It does not hurry.
3: There is a want in the stores: {task}. You have hands. Use them.
The Court asks, which is a courtesy. {task}, guest. Do not make the Court ask twice.
Bring {task} and the Court will count it in your favour. The Court counts carefully.
You have proved less troublesome than expected. A task, then: {task}. Do not make it your last.
The Court has begun to think of you when the stores run low. Bring {task}, and be thought of kindly.
A small errand, guest, and the Court's attention will follow you down the road: {task}.
I hesitate to trust a stranger with the Court's needs. I hesitate a little less each visit. Bring {task}.
There is {task} to be fetched, and no one of rank to fetch it. You will do. That is high praise.
The Stewards keep a column marked 'wanted'. Your errand is in it: {task}. Move it, if you can, to the column marked 'received'.
Take your time with {task}, but not too much. The Court is patient the way a drawn bow is patient.
Bring {task} and I will have your name spoken at council. I speak very little at council. Weigh that.
For the Court: {task}. For you: a better seat in the Court's regard. It is a fair exchange, by the Court's reckoning.
