A simple want, simply stated: {task}. Complicate it and I shall be displeased.
6: {player}, the Court has a task fit for you: {task}. Not beneath you. Not quite.
Bring {task}, if you would. The Court has learned you are reliable. Do not unlearn it for us.
A small matter: {task}. The thralls could see to it, eventually. You will see to it sooner.
{player}, would you bring {task}? I say 'would' because I wish to hear you say you will.
A thrall would fetch {task} and tell me nothing. You will fetch it and tell me everything. I know which I prefer.
The Court needs {task}. I need an excuse to see you return. Between us we have a task.
It is {task} this season. Last season it was something worse. You are fortunate in your timing and, I think, in your friends.
I have put your name beside {task} in the tally already. Do not make a liar of the Stewards.
Bring {task}, and I shall have the Riftguards stand a little straighter when you pass. It is the most I can arrange, and I assure you it is not nothing.
A quiet request: {task}. A quiet reward: the Court will not ask where you got it.
Tell me when you set out for {task}. I shall pretend to be surprised when you return so soon.
Bring {task}. You have done greater things for the Court's enemies. Do one small thing for the Court's friends.
A Steward has asked for {task}. The council does not know I am asking you. It will be our small conspiracy.
If you tire of errands, say so. I shall find another way to keep you near. But first, {task}.
9: I would trust only you with this, {player}: {task}. The Court will know who brought it.
We need {task}. I say 'we'. It is not a word the Court spends on guests.
Bring {task} when you can. When, {player}. Not if. The Court knows you now.
Ask me what the Court needs and I will say 'you'. Ask me what the stores need and I will say {task}.
Bring {task}, {player}. It is no longer a service. I think we are both too fond of the habit to call it anything else.
I would send no other. I would go myself, if I could be spared. Since I cannot: {task}.
The Stewards ask for {task}. I told them you would see to it. They did not question me. That, from a Steward, is love.
Bring {task}, if the road is kind. If it is not kind, bring yourself. The Court will manage without the rest.
There is a place near the dais where your name has been kept warm. It will be warmer with {task}.
I have a request. It is {task}. It is also an excuse: I wish to hear what has happened on your road since we last spoke.
The Court has asked for {task}. I asked that it be you. I used a word the Lord dislikes: 'please'.
Go and gather {task}, then come back and tell me a lie about how difficult it was. I will pretend to believe it.
Every errand I send you on is a small thread I tie to your hand so that you must return. This one is {task}. I have run out of knots, not reasons.
Bring {task}. After that, stay a while. The Court has no order for it, and I am making one.

0: You return empty-handed. {task}, guest. The Court has not forgotten. The Court never forgets.
Where is {task}? Ah. Nowhere. Go.
The stores still lack {task}. Do not stand here as though standing were service.
I asked for {task}. I look at your hands and find the request unanswered.
You have come to me with questions. I have no use for questions. I have a use for {task}.
Empty-handed guests are tolerated. Empty-handed servants are not. Decide which you are.
The Stewards have already written 'pending' beside your name. Do not make them reach for a harsher word.
Return when you carry {task}. Until then you are conversation, and the Court has plenty.
Do you imagine the Court asks for its amusement? Bring {task}, guest. It was not a figure of speech.
I do not repeat my wants more than twice. This is the second time. Count carefully.
Counted: you, one. Counted: {task}, none. The sum is unsatisfactory.
The Court expects errands to be done, not discussed. Go and gather {task}.
Somewhere in the world is {task}. You have not been to it. The Court notes the geography of your failures.
Do not mistake the Court's silence for patience. We are merely composing the next sentence. It begins: {task}.
3: Still no {task}. The Court's patience is long, guest, but it is not wide.
I see no {task} in your hands. I see a great deal of air.
The Court asked for {task}. The Court is still asking.
No {task} yet, guest? The Court understands that roads are long. It understands little else, and that little is shrinking.
I am not impatient. I am merely, as you see, very still. Bring {task}.
A short delay is forgiven. A long delay is remembered. You are somewhere in the middle, and I am deciding which way to lean.
Back already? Perhaps you missed the Gate. It is a fine Gate. Go and earn another look at it, with {task}.
The tally is patient. The Steward is patient. I am the least patient of the three, and I am only slightly impatient.
Consider the errand a puzzle: where is {task}, and how far is it from here? The Court has every faith in your answer.
If the errand is too hard, say so. The Court prefers honest failure to silent delay. We shall not like it, but we shall prefer it.
You wear the face of one who has not yet found {task}. I know the face. The Stewards wear it when the ledger will not close.
The council asked after {task}. I said you were seeing to it. Do not make a liar of me. I am out of practice.
Waiting is a skill, guest, and you are not yet good at it. Practise somewhere else, with {task} in hand.
I will not ask again today. I will ask again tomorrow. The Court has an excellent memory for tomorrow.
6: You have not brought {task} yet. Unlike you. Is something amiss in your world?
The tally still wants {task}, {player}. I will wait. I am good at waiting.
No {task} yet? The thralls are beginning to look smug. They should not be able to.
No {task}? Then you have been busy, or lost, or both. I would hear which, if you care to tell me.
I am not disappointed. I would like that noted. I am merely arranging my face into a shape that says otherwise.
Take your time, {player}. I am being polite. The Steward is being less polite on my behalf.
The stores are still waiting for {task}. The stores are used to it. They have been waiting for things since before the stone.
I hope the road has been kind. I hope it has been interesting. I hope you remember to collect {task} somewhere in the middle of it.
A little longer, then. I have rearranged my afternoon around your return. It did not take long. I have no afternoons.
You are not late. You are exactly as late as I expected, which is to say, in time.
Fetch {task} when it suits you, {player}. It suits the Court to see you again either way.
I admit to counting the days. Do not tell the Steward, who counts them aloud, and it is a very dull sound.
If anything stands in the road to {task}, remove it. If it will not be removed, tell me its name. The Court has opinions about names.
I looked for you from the wall. I saw only thralls. Come back with {task} and give the thralls something to look at.
9: Take what time you need for {task}. The Court has an age. You, I think, have rather less.
There is a place in the stores kept for {task}. It is empty. It is waiting for you, as are we.
Not yet, {player}? No matter. When you bring {task}, bring it yourself. The Court likes to see it handed over.
Still no {task}? I am glad. It means you have been somewhere worth being, and will have a story for the lack.
You owe the Court {task}. You owe me nothing at all. Keep the two accounts separate, if you can; the Stewards are nervous about it.
No need to hurry, {player}. I have waited longer for lesser things, and they did not arrive with news.
Not yet? Then linger, and tell me the road. The Court has waited for {task} this long, and I have waited for you longer.
Come back when you are able. I shall be here. I am always here. It is both the Court's great strength and its great sorrow.
The Stewards ask me daily whether {task} has arrived. I tell them it arrives when you do. They find that unscientific. I find it the only accurate thing I say.
The Court may not forgive a delay. I do, in advance. I shall see that the Court's voice in this hall is difficult to hear.
A thrall asked after you this morning, in its way. It stood a little longer at the Gate than its orders strictly required. Bring {task}, and bring it a story.
I would rather you came back safe and short of {task} than whole of it and hurt. I have said this in my own manner. Please hear it in yours.
There is no hurry in the Court's heart. There is a great hurry in the Steward's. I have asked the Steward to practise breathing.
Do you know what I do while I wait for you, {player}? I stand where you will come through the Gate and I look as though I am not looking. I am excellent at it.

0: It is delivered. The Court notes it. Do not expect thanks. Expect to be remembered.
Adequate. More than most strangers manage before we kill them.
*the brow-eyes blink, slowly, in sequence* The service is received.
Delivered: {task}. The Stewards will count it. If the count is short you will hear from them. If it is long you will hear nothing, which is the Court's thanks.
Received: {task}. Entered in the tally. Dismissed from the errand, not from the Court.
So the guest is capable of the simplest thing: to fetch, and to return. The Court has put away its surprise.
The stores take {task} gladly. Your hands are free. Try not to fill them with trouble.
You did what was asked. That is rarer than you think. Do not wait for praise; wait for the next request.
Delivered. The Court has no word for 'thank you', but several for 'noted'. This is the mildest of them.
Counted twice, as is the custom, and found whole: {task}. You may go on living.
A Steward will write that you came, that you gave, and that you left without incident. Many guests achieve only the first.
The debt is discharged. Do not mistake the discharge for an invitation to linger.
Adequate, guest. The Court has seen better. It has also seen worse, and the worse did not leave by the Gate.
It is done. Stand at ease, which in this hall means stand slightly less stiffly.
3: Well done, guest. That is not a phrase I use. Mark it.
The thralls will stack it in the yards. Your name will be stacked beside it, in the Court's memory.
Received. The Court has fewer reasons to doubt you than it did.
That is {task}, in full. The Court expected you to fall a little short. I am not displeased to be wrong.
You return with what was asked. I enter it in your favour, which in the Court's ledgers is a thin column. It is growing.
The council was told. The council said 'good'. It said it as one speaks of weather. Take what comfort you can.
Well done. I notice I have now said so twice in your presence. I do not intend to make a habit of it.
Received. The thralls will stack it, the Stewards will count it, and I, uniquely, will note that you did it without complaint.
The Court's stores are fuller by {task} and the Court's opinion of you is fuller by a little. Both are noted.
You are punctual and thorough. These are rare in guests and common in thralls. Take it as the highest compliment or the lowest. Either serves.
It is as asked. I find I have nothing to criticise. This discomforts me. I shall find something by your next visit.
A guest who returns with {task} is a guest who returns. I find the second more valuable than the first.
The Stewards approve. They have never used the word before. They used a number, which for them is the same.
I accept it on behalf of the Court. The Court accepts it on behalf of no one, which is the Court's greatest courtesy.
6: You do not waste the Court's time. The Court finds it refreshing.
Good. Exactly as asked, no less. You learn our ways quickly, {player}.
This will be told in the Throne Hall. Briefly. But it will be told.
You brought {task} as if it were nothing. I know it was not nothing. I know what the road costs. I shall not say more, only that I know.
There. The Court has what it asked and I have what I wanted: the sight of you coming through the Gate.
You brought {task}. And, in the same breath, you. The second gives me more pleasure than the first, which I will deny to anyone who asks.
I set aside a small portion of the Court's regard for each service of yours. It has become a considerable portion. I am a prudent saver.
I told the Steward you would bring {task} by evening. The Steward doubted. I have been insufferable all afternoon.
You have a gift for doing the right thing without being seen to do it. The Court prefers it. So do I.
Done. And well done, which I notice I said without being forced. The Court would call that a weakness. I call it a good watch.
The thralls straightened a little when you came in. I do not think they know they did it. I noticed.
Another service, another thread. The council asked who keeps the Court so well supplied. I said, 'a friend'. I was not lying.
It is received, and so are you, in whatever ways the Court allows. Stand beside the line with me a moment, {player}. Do not cross it. Just stand.
Each time you do this I begin composing a sentence of thanks, and each time I abandon it halfway. Perhaps next time.
9: As ever, {player}. The Court has stopped wondering whether you will return. It wonders only when.
Received, and remembered. You have filled a good many of our shelves, guest.
If the Court gave thanks, this would earn them. Take, instead, our regard. It is rarer.
Received, {player}. And since no one is near enough to hear: thank you. There. I have said it. It is out and cannot be recalled.
You do the Court's work so well that I have begun to forget it is the Court's. I think of it as ours.
I stopped counting your services long ago. The Stewards count them for me. I merely keep the sum, and it is always the same: more than I deserve.
It is received, and so, I think, is something else. I do not know what to call it. I will let the Stewards enter it as 'miscellaneous'.
If every guest were like you, the Court would have no need of thralls. I am glad they are not. I would miss having you to myself.
There is a custom in the oldest law of presenting a returning servant with a cup. We have no cups. I give you this sentence instead: you are welcome here.
I would give you a rank, if ranks could be given for what you are. Since they cannot, I give you this: a place at the dais edge, always, and my attention.
Of all the guests, yours is the return I hear from three halls away. The Stewards have asked how. I told them it is a matter of sound. It is not.
The Stewards wished to enter {task} under 'service'. I wished to enter it under 'friendship'. I overruled them. Then I overruled myself.
It is always the same: you bring {task}, and I find I would have waited twice as long. Do not take that as encouragement. Take it as a warning that I am unreliable.
Well, {player}. The Court has received. The Court has been enriched. The Court, for once, has nothing to add, and will say nothing, and will enjoy saying it.

0: *every eye along the brow opens wide* Where did you... No. Do not tell me. The Court accepts this.
This is a gift fit for a throne. The Court is surprised. It dislikes being surprised. Not today.
You understand what the Court values. That is rarer than the thing itself.
*the oldest eye on the brow opens first, then the rest* ...This belongs in the Throne Hall. Who gave you leave to carry it?
No thrall will touch it. The Steward will, with a cloth, and with a witness.
You set a treasure in my claws as though it were a pebble. Do you know what you have done?
A guest who knows what to carry is a danger of its own kind. I shall watch you more closely.
*the shards over the brow draw together, tight as a fist* Tell no one you owned this. Tell no one you gave it.
The Court has lost such things to thieves and to time. It did not expect one to return in a stranger's hands.
It was the Court's by right. It is yours to give only because you reached the door first. Mark the difference.
I will not say we are pleased. I will say that eyes will turn to this tonight, and not turn away.
You are still a stranger here. This is not a stranger's gift. It is a debt beginning.
The Court is rarely given what it wants. It is not certain how to arrange its face.
*every eye on the brow settles on the gift, none on you* ...Go on. Breathe. The Court is occupied.
Do not ask what it is worth. The Court does not put a price on what it means to keep.
3: *the shards over the brow flare* Yes. This. The Court will not forget it.
A worthy tribute. The Lord will hear of this before the hour is out.
No envoy of the old days brought such gifts. Who taught you our tastes?
The Steward will enter this in the black-covered ledger. Very little earns the black cover.
A plinth in the Hall of Keeping has stood empty since the cities were sealed. It will not stand empty tonight.
You find what the Court has lost, guest. I begin to suspect it is not luck.
*the brow-eyes open outward from the centre, a pair at a time* Yes. This was worth the long walk.
The Court is used to taking. You are teaching it, against its will, to receive.
A count of gifts is kept at the foot of the throne. Yours has just moved up it.
I should like to keep this for myself. Law says the Court's. Pride says mine. Law wins, and I resent it.
Few guests think to bring the Court what it truly prizes. I wonder who whispered it to you.
It will be shown at the next council. The council will pretend not to be moved.
A tribute of rank, from a guest of rising rank. We note the direction in which you climb.
{neighbour} will hear of this before the next watch. News cannot be stopped in a Citadel, only chosen.
Remarkable. Do not look pleased with yourself, guest. It makes the shards itch.
6: You honour {village}, {player}. The Court finds it can say so without choking.
This goes to the Throne Hall, not the stores. That is where such things belong.
*a long silence, every eye fixed on the gift* ...Well chosen.
You need not bring such things to be welcome, {player}. But I will not pretend the Court is unmoved.
I will carry this to the Hall of Keeping myself, past the stair, past the guard, past every curious eye.
I have been given many things in my years. Few were given for no reason beyond good will.
You choose gifts as the Court chooses allies: for what they mean, not what they cost.
*the claws close over the gift with great care* It will lie where the light of the crystal can find it.
Every reader of omens will beg to see it. I will tell them to wait a night. A gift deserves one night of simple admiring.
The Court cannot give thanks. I can, quietly, with the door shut. Consider the door shut.
There is a place near the throne for such tributes. A small plate with your name has been cut for it. The plate is new.
The council says you are buying favour. Let it. I have never seen favour so well worth the price.
The finest tribute {village} has received since the old envoys. I intend that as the highest praise I own.
You know what the Court wants, {player}. Best not tell the others how well.
Give the Court its joys often enough and it may forget to be proud. Do not hurry that. Pride suits us.
9: {player}, you have a gift for gifts. The Court will speak of this one at council.
Again you bring the Court what it loves. One might almost think you were fond of us.
This will be kept as long as {village} stands. That is a very long time.
*every brow-eye closes at once, in something near a smile* You spoil the Court, {player}. It is unaccustomed. It will adjust.
I am to say that the Court is pleased. I am to say it sternly. I cannot find the stern voice.
When they ask what you wanted for this, I shall say I do not know. It will be the only honest answer anyone in {village} has given in an age.
No one has given the Court so much who owed it so little. No one but you.
I will not call it too much. I will only say the stores are beginning to feel like yours.
A treasure and a friend in a single visit. The Court is not built for abundance.
Whatever you ask next, {player}, I find I am already inclined to grant it. Dangerous, that you should know.
*a low, warped sound that in anyone else would be a chuckle* I have outlived a thousand gifts. This one I shall outlive more slowly.
I accept with something that, among the Shulkin, would be called gladness. Do not repeat the word in the halls.
The thralls will bear it to the Hall of Keeping with every care. I told them it was yours. They have never walked so gently.
Fine, {player}. The finest. I say so as the Court, and I say so as myself, and for once the two agree.
Keep giving like this and I shall have to build a wing for you. I have already chosen the stone.

0: Acceptable. The Court takes it.
Sound tribute. The stores will have it.
Hm. Not without worth. You may set it down.
For the stores. Serviceable.
The thralls will carry it in. You may go on being tolerated.
A tribute at last. The ledger has gone a long while without a new line.
It is what the Court uses. That is the highest compliment I can pay a thing of yours.
*a claw takes it, turns it once, and sets it aside* Acceptable. Do not expect a feast.
Fair weight, fair make. You may keep your head a while longer.
The Court counts it. The count is small, but it is not zero. Begin there.
Few guests bring the right things on early visits. You brought half right. Continue.
It will be useful. I do not say pleasing. I say useful, which is rarer in guests.
We take it. We note that you brought it unasked. The Court prefers unasked.
Put it on the stair. There. The thralls will lift it when you are gone.
A lesser gift than the throne deserves. A larger one than I expected from you.
3: A fitting offering. The Court notes your judgement.
Well chosen. The thralls will carry it to the stores, and you will be remembered for it.
This pleases the Court. Do not let it go to your head.
You are learning the Court's tastes. Your name is being scratched into a wider column of the ledger.
Well made, well meant. The Court takes both, though it prefers the first.
This will serve the Citadel. Remember it when your gifts go unthanked. They are never unnoticed.
*two brow-eyes dip toward the tribute* A fair offering. The council need not hear of it. I will tell {neighbour} anyway.
I had a use for something like this and no one to ask. You asked nothing. You simply came with it.
The stores of {village} are a little fuller for you. The stores keep faith with those who fill them.
It is not a treasure. It is better: the sort of thing the Court actually runs on.
A guest who gives what is wanted, not what is shiny. The Court respects that more than glitter.
Fitting. I will not call it lovely. It is useful, and I am not a Shulkin.
The thralls bow lower as your gifts pass. They do not know why. I think they feel the weight is honest.
Set aside for the next mending of the east wall. Walls are repaired with gifts as well as with stone.
The Court has begun to expect your tribute. Take that as a warning, or an honour. Both are accurate.
6: Generous, as is becoming your habit.
The Court accepts, and is not displeased. Treasure the phrase.
You know what serves {village}. Good.
Generous again, {player}. The ledger has stopped being surprised by you and started to be bored.
You bring what we need before we know to need it. I have watched whole councils with less foresight.
I am glad of it, {player}. Not the thing so much as the bringing.
*a claw rests briefly on the gift, as one rests it on a shoulder* Well chosen.
The Court has few friends beyond the Gate. It is starting to count the ones who bring tribute.
Among the old envoys, a guest who returned with tribute was offered a seat. We have no seat. Accept the sentiment.
Take comfort, {player}: your gifts are used. The Citadel stands a little straighter for each one.
You could keep these and spend them in your own world. That you do not is noticed. That you do not mind is noticed more.
A fine piece. It will be set where visitors can see it, and I will tell them who brought it.
Even the guard on the stair did not sneer when you passed with this. From the guard, that is a banner and a drum.
I will say it plainly, since you have earned plain speech: this was kindly done.
I stopped inspecting your gifts for hidden insults a visit ago. Trust is an expensive habit, {player}.
9: Fine tribute, {player}. The Court expected no less, and you did not give less.
Set it with the rest. You have quite a pile in our stores by now.
Useful, and well meant. The Court notices both.
Another for the pile. The pile now has a name, and the name is yours. The tally-keepers are embarrassed.
The thralls hear you coming and ready their arms. They have never been so eager for anyone.
I used to count your tributes. Now I count the days between them. It is a poorer sum, and a more honest one.

The council meets at the dark hour and argues till the dark hour again. We attend the first speech and the last. Between them is a silence we have earned.

There were Lords before us whose names are cut from the floor. We keep their thrones swept. A Lord who forgets the fallen soon joins them.
Your world has a sun. We are told it is one great eye that opens each morning. We find that unbearably forward of it.
We do not hate the Shulkin, {player}. One does not hate the record of one's mistakes. One merely keeps it shut.
Once a Lord could end a quarrel by lifting a claw. Now the quarrel must be written down in three copies. The Court has grown tired and fussy.
We keep a chair near the dais that nobody sits in. It was a rival's. We keep it to remind us that rivals are worth the furniture.
The Seers say the void is wide. The Voidmarshals say the void is a wall. We think the void is a crowd, waiting politely.
There is a Citadel beyond the rim that calls our spire short. Do you know what they say of our throne? We do. We keep the copies.
Few have ever asked what we want, guest. You may, if you like. We will say we want nothing. It will be very nearly true.
Every Lord is given a hall, a crown and a number of eyes. None is given a reason. We have been looking for ours.
We were taught that a Lord who yawns is already dethroned. We have not yawned in a very long time. It is the most tiring thing we do.
Listen to the hall when it is silent, guest. It hums. Our crown and the great doors hum in the same key. We had thought it chance.
The thralls lay obsidian in the same patterns they laid before we were Lord. We have never asked them why. We suspect they do not know.
The Dragon made our fortunes. A hand that holds the world by its throat has no need of manners. Now the hand is open, and we are learning manners again.
We could have you written in the Roll of Arrivals, {player}. Instead you are written in our memory, which is longer and less forgiving.
A visitor once asked if we were lonely. We kept them at the Gate three days to think on the question. They never returned with an answer.
Our Riftguards say you walk like one who expects to be struck and has decided not to mind. We have decided to approve.
There is a saying in the Court: a Lord is a stone the council has agreed to lean on. We lean back, now and then, to test them.
6: We have watched you keep our law. We have watched closely. We find little fault.
Our ships still lie moored at the dead cities, a seal aboard each. You found one. Fate or theft. We do not mind which.
The Court is old, guest, and the old do not change. We are not changing. We are, perhaps, adjusting.
Ask what you will. We will answer what we will. That is the shape of every audience.
Our thralls haul stone from every world. You are the first stone that ever walked to us on its own.
We have grown used to your step. It is a poor thing to say of a guest, and a great one to say of a Lord.
Once we walked the central island at the head of a procession, and the purpur cities lit their lamps as we passed. It was the only time we were ever welcomed.
The weight of the crown is not the shards. It is the eight eyes. Each must be kept open, and each must be kept honest.
We have been Lord so long that our own name has begun to sound like a title.
At the dark hour, when the hall empties, we count the shards of the crown. We have never lost one. We count anyway.
A Lord is supposed to be feared. We have managed that. We are told that being loved is a different craft, and a harder one. We have no apprentices.
You have never begged us for anything, {player}. Service is trade; tribute is manners. We think that is why we tolerate you.
The thralls bring us the world's stone and never its news. A guest brings news. Tell us something small. A bird, a leaf, a quarrel in a village.
The council called you a risk. The Seers called you an omen. We called you a visitor, and the Herald wrote it down, which is a first.
Sometimes we climb to the spire when the hall empties and stand near the crystal. It is not a ritual. It is a thing to do with the claws.
A Lord's word is law only while the Lord can be heard. Our voice is quieter than it was. The Herald makes up the difference.
We do not forgive, guest. We simply stop counting. The difference is thinner than you think and wider than the Court allows.
If the Court were merciful it would be weak, and if it were weak it would be gone. We are not unkind by choice. We are unkind by arithmetic.
The Voidhounds sleep on the steps of the dais. We have never told a hound to move. It is one of the few courtesies we pay unasked.
We have been called cruel by wiser tongues than yours, and we were not bothered. We find we would be bothered if you said it.
There was a Lord before us whose crystal went dark. They went down the stair beneath the hall. We keep the door above it oiled. We do not know why.
We have learned your world's word for it: tired. We found it in a Shulkin record. It was the first Shulkin word we ever found useful.
Can you hear the hall, guest? Under the hum? That is the sound of eight eyes, tired. We do not hear it unless we have company.
We recall the first day of our reign. We recall the crown being set. We recall that it was a great deal lighter.
Anyone may take a throne. To keep it one needs a reason to wake. We have lately found a few, and one of them is a guest's visit.
9: We have had envoys, servants, rivals and enemies. Never a friend. We are told this is what one looks like.
If {village} fell, we would want you to have been elsewhere. Make of that what you will. We will not say it twice.
You silenced our weapon and then kept our law. We have no precedent for you, {player}. We are writing one.
The crown is heavy, guest. It is lighter on the days you come. Do not repeat that.
Guests may not sit in the presence of the throne. You may sit. Do not ask us why.
{player}, we have never said this to anyone: the crown is not the heaviest thing in the hall. The heaviest thing is being the only one nobody may ask how they fare.
We asked the Seers whether the crystal would go dark in our reign. They said they could not see. It is the only honest answer a Seer has ever given us.
We still hear the lamps, some nights. Not the sound of them. The sound of their absence. It is like the hush after a bell.
There is a rival who calls us butcher. Before you, we would have answered with a fleet. Now we answer with a letter, and its last lines are nearly kind.
We have taught the hounds to lie on the steps and not growl at you. It took a month. We asked them kindly. Do not tell the Voidmarshals the Lord asks.
If you ever tire of your world, there is a seat. Not the throne. A small one, near the glass of the Seers' Spire, where the stars are loudest. We have it kept.
We were told a Lord has no friends, only instruments. We chose, in the end, to be wrong about that.
You have seen us tired, {player}. Few have. The Court sees a crown. You see the one beneath it. Keep it between us.
Sometimes we sit on the throne with our eyes closed, and we think of rain. We have never felt rain. It is the gentlest thing we know of.
Our predecessors cut 'Rule well' into the arm of the throne, where only the one who sits can read it. We read it each dark hour. Some nights it says something else.
We have outlived every promise we made, {player}, except one: that we would not be the Lord who let the Court die quietly. We keep that one.
When you leave, the hall echoes. We never noticed it echoed before. It has begun to trouble us, which we think is a compliment.
Ask us anything. Not the one thing. Anything else. We find we wish to be asked, for once, by someone who does not need the answer.
Had the world been kinder we might have been a gardener. We do not know where the thought came from. It arrived in the dark hour and sat on the arm of the throne.
A Lord's last duty is to choose who will keep the crown. We have looked at the Court for an age and found only ambition. We would like the next to have a friend.
We keep a ledger of those we trusted. It is one page. For a long time it was blank. Your name is written at the foot, in our own claw, where nobody checks.
The old tongue has a word for one who keeps a lamp lit for another. It is not 'guest' and it is not 'host'. We may teach it to you.
The crystal burns violet now, not white. The Seers think it a failing. We think it a mood. We have decided to hold to that.
Whatever the Court asks of you, {player}, know this: the throne would rather you came back whole than came back with the tribute.
We will be remembered as the Lord who loosed the Dragon. We would like a second line, in a smaller hand: and who kept a friend.

0: Our law is older than our hall. We could not break it if we wished. We do not wish. Yet.
Guest-law is our word given. We break our word for no one. You would be wise to break yours for no one too.
Law is not cruelty, guest. Law is a wall that does not move. You will find you can lean on it, if you do not push.
The Herald reads the seal. The Riftguards stand by. The throne listens. That is guest-law in its entirety, and it has never been improved.
Break the law and we shall not shout. We shall not even rise. We shall merely open the Gate and the Court will do the rest.
A law that bends is a suggestion. We have never made suggestions.
Every law of the Court was written because something went wrong. Remember that when you find one absurd.
We did not write guest-law for your protection. We wrote it so that the Court would never have to feel it had been unfair.
6: We made the law. We keep the law. We expect the same of you, and so far you have not disappointed us.
Do you know how long a law lives? Longer than the one who wrote it, always. Ours has outlived many Lords and will outlive us.
We have broken a good many things in our reign. Never law. Law is the one thing in the Citadel that is truly the Court's. The rest is stone.
Guest-law cuts both ways, {player}. If the Court wronged you, the law would bind us. It would be very awkward. We would do it.
You asked whether law ever softens. It does not. It is we who soften toward those who have kept it. A small, private amendment.
The old Lords thought law a chain. We think it a handrail. You may hold it a while.
Our law says a guest may not be struck within the walls. It does not say what a Lord may feel about a guest. That part we write ourselves.

0: We loosed it. We would loose it again. You killed it. We have not decided whether to thank you or to punish you.
The Dragon was our voice over the central island. Now the island is silent, and we speak from here.
The Dragon obeyed one word, once. Over the ages it obeyed it less. A weapon that tires of its wielder is worse than no weapon.
Do not praise us for the Dragon's death, guest. And do not blame us for its life. We have heard both. Neither is useful.
We watched it rise from the central island. We watched it turn. We watched the lamps of the first purpur city go dark. We did not look away. A Lord does not.
You expected remorse, perhaps. The Court does not keep it. We keep the record. The record has no feelings, which is its great virtue.
The Voidmarshals wished to take back the central island when the Dragon fell. We forbade it. An empty throne is a trap. We know. We have laid several.
Every Lord of this Court sat in the Dragon's shadow, in a sense. We sit now in its absence. We find the second the colder.
9: We called it once, and it came, and the cities burned. Then one day it would not come. You ended what we could no longer end.
{player}, some nights we dream of the Dragon, though we are told we do not dream. It is not the burning we see. It is the way it turned its head to look at us before it went.
We ordered it. You ended it. Between us the Court has a debt it cannot name. We do not pay debts we cannot name. We are... considering it.
We kept the first scale it shed. It lies in the hall of the crystal. It is still warm at the edges. We have never told the Seers.
Had you not ended the Dragon, we would have had to, some day. We lacked the word to unsay what we had said. You had a blade. A blade is simpler.
Some here wanted you dead for it. We stood on the dais and said that it was ours to end, and it was ended, and they should be quiet. They were.
Thank you, {player}. We have said it. The crystal has not cracked. The hall has not fallen. We find we survive it.

0: *the crystal in the crown dims* You ask the throne that? We will forget you asked. Once.
You ask for the one thing a Lord is sworn to keep. Ask for a hound, a favour, a ship. Not that.
*all eight eyes close, and the crown stills* There is a question that ends audiences. You have found it.
We are the Court. We are what we are. How, and whence, is a locked door, and we gave the key away.
Leave it, guest. The void will keep it better than either of us.
That is a closed book. We do not know every page of it ourselves, and what we do know we have chosen to forget.
6: There is one thing the Court will never tell you, {player}, and you have just asked it. Ask anything else.
We could tell you. Then the Court would have to unmake you, and we would have to watch. We are fond of you. We shall not make ourselves watch.
Look at the thralls, guest, and look at us. Then look at the Seers. Three kinds of eyes. Ask which came first. We do not know.
Our oldest memory is of waking in the dark with the Court already about us. We were not told how. We did not ask. Asking is where the unmaking starts.
Your world's dark places are very full, guest. Full of eyes, we are told. We take no view.
A Lord is the keeper of the secret, not its author. We guard a door we have never opened. It is possible there is nothing behind it. That is the part that frightens us.
Do not ask the Seers a second time. The first answer is a kindness. The second is a wound.

0: We take note of you, guest. Few are noted from the throne.
Our eyes rest on you a moment longer than they did. Count that a rise in the world.
The throne has marked you, {player}. A small mark. A scratch upon the arm of the chair. It may fade.
*one of the eight eyes turns and stays on you* You rise a step in the Court's regard, guest. Mind the next one.
Your name has reached the far end of the hall. The Steward has put it in a smaller ledger than the others, but a ledger.
We asked ourselves whether to be pleased. The question took us a full breath. That is a long time for a Lord.
Hm. The Court's regard is a staircase, guest, and you have set a foot upon the lowest step. Climb or fall.
5: The throne regards you, {player}. Rise higher, and it may regard you with something like warmth. It never has.
We have spoken your name at council. The Voidmarshals objected. We overruled them.
You rise, {player}. The throne notices. The throne does not smile. It notices.
Our council now disputes your name, which is how one knows a name matters. Half call you a friend. Half call you a lesson.
*the crown of shards drifts a hand's breadth lower* A courtesy. Count it. We seldom spend them.
Of account, of standing, of weight. The Court has many words for those it cannot ignore, {player}. We are teaching them to you one at a time.
We are told the Voidmarshals have stopped putting your name on the watch-list. We did not ask them to. We merely did not forbid it.
10: Friend of the Crown. We have never said those words to one not of the Court. We say them to you.
*the end crystal in the crown blazes* Hear us, {village}: {player} is Friend of the Crown, now and while we stand.
{player}. Friend of the Crown. We have spoken it into the throne. The throne does not forget.
We have not named a friend since the crown was set. The word has waited in our mouth a very long time. It tasted of dust, and then of something else.
*all eight eyes open, steady, and do not close* There is no higher station we can give you. If there were, we would be inventing it.
Let the Herald cry it and the Seers write it and the crystal burn it: the Lord of {village} has a friend. May it vex everyone who ought to be vexed.
You may come and go in this hall as the hounds do, {player}, which is to say: unasked, and always welcome.

0: Our kennels hold a pup whose eyes are already on you. We give it. Take it, {player}.
A hound of {village}, from the throne's own hand. No guest has been given one in an age. Kneel, and receive it.
We grant you a Voidhound. It will hunt for you, guard you, and remind every Endarch whose favour you carry.
You have earned something we do not sell and seldom give. A hound of the Court. Will you take it?
Our kennel-keeper tells us a pup has refused three names and three collars. We think it is waiting for you. Will you take it?
There is a pup in the kennels that growls at every Riftguard who bends to it, and wags at your name. We find this significant.
We have bred hounds for longer than your kind has bred anything. Take the best pup of this litter, {player}, and prove the breeding true.
A Court does not give gifts, only trusts. The pup is a trust. We offer it.
Take a hound of {village}, {player}. Should you ever be lost beyond the Gate, it will find the way back to us, and you with it.
We are told the pup rifts to the door each time the Herald cries your name. It is time it had you to rift to.
The kennels have chosen. We do not overrule the kennels. Come, take what the kennels have chosen.
A hound at your heel will say what no Herald need cry: that you stand in the Court's regard. Will you carry such a sign?
We rarely offer. We have not offered in an age. We offer now. Do not hesitate; we dislike being left waiting with a gift in our claws.
Four generations of our best blood in one small pup. We give it to you, {player}. Mind it.
Our hounds hunt in silence and guard in silence. This one has found a friend in you. We have decided to make it formal.
Come to the kennel gate, guest. A pup is there with nothing in its head but you.
It will forgive you a great deal, {player}. It will forgive nothing done to you. Take it.
Let it be said in {village}: the throne gave, and the guest received. Let it be said it was fitting.
The pup in the third stall will not eat unless the Gate is in sight. It has chosen you, guest. We do not argue with hounds.
A litter was born in our kennels under the dim crystal. One of them has your scent already, though it has never met you. Take it.
A Voidhound is the Court's loyalty in a small black coat. We give it to you, {player}. Be worthy of its trust.
Come, guest. The pup is small, and we will not have it handed down from the dais like a decree. It will be placed in your arms.
We seldom part with the kennels' get. For you we make an exception. Do not make it an error.
Our hounds have never needed a master, only a reason. We offer you the pup, and a reason with it. Take both.
It is yours. Its collar bears our mark. Its loyalty, from today, bears yours.
Take it. When it is grown, strangers will fear it as they fear us. Use that well.
The pup goes with you, {player}. Do not make us regret the stall we emptied.
There. A shard of {village} that walks at your heel. Guard it as we would.
*the pup is lowered from the dais into your arms* Hold it as you would hold a flame that does not burn.
It will outgrow its collar before it outgrows its curiosity. Loosen the one; feed the other.
The shard above its back is its first. It will grow more as it grows. Do not trim them.
A Voidhound sleeps when its keeper sleeps and wakes when trouble does. Sleep easier, {player}.
It will hop through small rifts when startled. Do not be alarmed. It is only following you, by a shorter path.
It knows the smell of our halls. Let it carry that smell into your world, so that your world knows who guards your back.
Do not let strangers pet it. It will allow them once, and then take the hand.
We have given Voidmarshals less than this. Do not mention it to the Voidmarshals.
Its name is yours to give. Let it be a good one. Names outlast collars.
There. It is yours, {player}, and you are, in the only way our law allows, ours. A little.
It will find you wherever you go. Do not be surprised. It has been told you are worth finding.
The kennel-keeper is already weeping, in the way kennel-keepers do. Do not look back at them.
Keep it fed, keep it fierce, keep it close. And when it grows, show it the void. It will want to see its home.
Go gently on the stair. It has never seen one it could not leap, and it is very small.
*the pup is set in your arms, warm and heavier than it looks* It has your scent now. It will not forget.
Name it as you wish, {player}. The kennels name them Shard, Ash and Quiet. You are not bound by the kennels.
Feed it meat. It will be loyal to the meat first, and to you after, and in time it will not notice the difference.
Go. Show the pup the world past the Gate. We are told there is a great deal of it.
The collar is the Court's. A leash would be an insult. The pup will stay at your heel because it wishes to.
A hound of {village}. When it howls, we shall know. The kennels keep an ear turned your way.
We gave you a hound already. We do not give twice.
Your hound is the Court's whole answer. Look at it, not at us.
One hound, {player}. Even a friend of the Crown is given only one.
We remember giving you a pup. We remember its face. Is it well?
Two hounds would be a pack, and a pack needs a leader. The leader here is already us.
You came for a hound and have one. Come for something else next time. The kennels are modest. The Court is not.
Ask the hound you have what it thinks of the idea. Hounds are blunt.
A second pup would only make the first jealous. We have seen it. It is not pretty.
We gave you our trust in a collar. Do not ask us to give it twice in the same hand.
The litters are for those who have none. You have one. Be content, as the hound is content.
We cannot give what is given. Look to your heel. It has been there all this while, waiting for you to notice.
We are not stingy, {player}. We are exact. There is a difference, and it is the difference between a Court and a market.
The kennels have a rule: one hound, one guest, one Citadel. We wrote it in a bad year. We keep it in good ones.
Another hound? No. A visit, a tale, a service: those we give freely. Hounds, only once.
Take your hound hunting in the outer dark. Perhaps it will find you something worth giving us in return.
Is there no hound at your heel? We gave you ours. One pup. That is the whole of a Lord's generosity.
The kennels are not a market, {player}. One hound, once. A second would require our dishonour.
We gave you the best of the litter and you ask for the second best? We are almost flattered.
Care for the hound you have. Its loyalty is not a thing the Court issues twice.
No more. The kennels will not be bled for a guest's appetite, however well liked the guest.
We have given what the throne gives once. Ask for something else, {player}. A story. A silence. We have both in plenty.
A hound from our kennels? You presume, guest. Earn more of our regard.
We do not give hounds to strangers we merely tolerate.
Ask again when the Court speaks your name with something other than suspicion.
Not yet. Perhaps never. Serve, and we will see.
A pup is trained for years to serve a hand it trusts. We have not yet decided you are a hand worth trusting.
The hounds growl at you in their sleep. It is not a good omen. Win them over, and win us over, and then ask.
We would sooner give you a glaive, {player}. A glaive does not need feeding, or forgiving.
Come to us after more service. A hound given early is a hound wasted.
Not today. The kennel-keeper would resign, and the kennel-keeper is irreplaceable. You, as yet, are not.
The pups are weaned on loyalty. You have not yet shown us any that we can feed them.
Ask us in a season of fewer strangers. Or ask us when you are fewer strangers.
Our regard for you is a small thing. A hound is a large one. We cannot trade the one for the other.
A guest who asks for a hound before earning a seat has misjudged both. Earn the seat.
You do not yet stand near enough to the dais to be given what sleeps upon its steps.
We are fond of that boldness, a little. We are not fond enough to give a Voidhound for it.
The pups will be here when you have deserved them. They are patient. They are, we remind you, the Court's.
Bring the Court more of its needs, and the kennels may find a spare place at your heel.
We said not yet. Take comfort in the 'yet'. We do not use the word lightly.
A hound is a vow with teeth. The Court does not make vows with guests it has barely met.
The pups sleep in the Lord's own shadow. They will not stir for a stranger. Neither will we.
Not yet, guest. The throne counts your visits, and the sum is small.
We have too few hounds and too many guests. You see the arithmetic.
A Voidhound's bite has weight in the Court. We give it only to a hand we trust. We do not trust yours. Yet.
Return when the Herald cries your name without sighing. Then we shall speak of kennels.
*the crystal in the crown dims* The throne has heard enough. Withdraw.
We grant audiences by the breath, guest, and you have spent yours. Go.
You are dismissed from the presence of Lord {name}. Do not turn your back until the dais is behind you.
Enough. When we wish to hear you again, the Herald will cry it.
*the crown of shards turns away from you, one fragment at a time* The throne has other business than you.
A Lord's attention is a lamp. It is lit for a moment, and it moves on. Go.
We have given you the time it takes the crystal to pulse thrice. You have had your thrice. Withdraw.
Your tongue has run its course. Let our silence run its own.
Return to the Gate, {player}. Leave by the way you came. Do not look at the hounds.
We are not offended. We are simply done. There is a difference, and only the Court is permitted to feel it.
The Voidmarshals wait. The Steward waits. You have been made to wait for no one. Be grateful, and go.
The audience ends where the light of the crystal ends. Step out of it.
We have heard enough. Let the guest be shown the stair, and let the stair be long.
We dismiss you with the usual courtesy, which is none. Leave.
*the shards of the crown rise a hand's breadth* The throne is weary. Withdraw.
We have no more words for you today. We spent them on the council, who deserved them less.
The audience is closed, {player}. Walk backward to the Gate, if you can. If you cannot, walk quickly.
That will do. The hall is an old thing and tires of echoes. Go.
We wish to be alone with the crystal. It does not interrupt. Leave us.
Lord {name} returns to the silence. Let the guest return to whatever noise they came from.
*the eyes close, left to right, all eight* We are not here. Do not look for us.
Enough, guest. There is a dust on the throne that must be allowed to settle. Go.
*the end crystal in the crown flares white* You raised a hand against the throne! The throne answers!
We read your seal, we let you speak, we let you live. Now we shall let you die.
Eight eyes saw it. Eight eyes remember. None will forgive.
You strike the Lord of {village}? In our own hall? Hounds! Glaives! To us!
Guest-law is ours to give and ours to take. We take it.
Our crown has stood through an age of war. It shall stand through yours, short as it is.
To the dais! The oathbreaker is at the throne! Let it not leave!
A guest struck its host. In the old tongue there is a word for that. Death is the translation.
We had thought better of you, {player}. We had thought of you at all. That was our error.
You have broken our law in our hall. We will break you in our yard.
Seize it! Alive, if it is quick. Dead, if it is not!
*the crown of shards rises, trembling* The throne has been struck. Nothing will be left of the striker!
Not a word. Not a plea. The time for speech is past, {player}. Take it!
*eight eyes open and burn* We struck the cities from the sky. We shall strike you from the earth!
Stand if you must. You will not stand long!
You will not cross the dais! You will not cross the hall! You will not cross anything again!
Our crystal watches, our hounds hunger, our eyes are on you! Prepare!
We are the Lord of {village}! We have buried worlds!
The Dragon was our hand. This is our fist!
Come to us, {player}! We have waited since the Dragon fell for something worth breaking!
Hounds! Glaives! The throne is awake!
Impudent! Impudent! IMPUDENT!
We will take the Eyes from your corpse and set them back in their reliquary!
Every blow you strike is a debt you cannot pay!
Our crown trembles at your insolence! Be ended by it!
The Lord does not step down from the dais. The Lord steps down for you. Be honoured, and die!
Dragon-slayer. I am {title} {name}. I have planned your death eleven ways. Speak.
You. State your business.
Dragon-slayer. You are inside my perimeter. State your reason.
Guest. I have counted your exits. There are two. Do not make me count one.
*plate grinding, the Voidmarshal turns from the war table* Speak. Quickly.
You walk into {village} as though it were a field. It is a fortress. Walk accordingly.
The seal is true, so you stand. Stand straighter.
Report, guest. Who sent you, what do you want, and how long will it take.
I am {title} {name}. You are an unscheduled arrival. I dislike those.
I watched you cross the causeway. You never checked your flanks. Begin again.
Hold. Hands where my Riftguards can see them. Now speak.
*a glance that measures you for a grave* Bearer. Well?
Mind the war table. Nothing on it is a toy, least of all the piece that looks like you.
3: The guest. Your guard was low at the Gate. Fix it.
{player}. Still alive. Good. Saves me a report.
{player}. Your approach was quieter this time. Better.
The guest. Your file has moved from the stack marked 'threats' to the stack marked 'unresolved'. Take heart.
Dragon-slayer. The Riftguards reported your step before the Herald cried it. They are learning you.
